title: Exile in Burma
hookLine: Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon

lines: A MAN IN WHITE, UNDER GUARD.
cards: A ship pulls away from the coast of India, heading east across the Bay of Bengal. On board, under guard, is a man in white who has never been tried for any crime.
He's being taken to Rangoon, in Burma, where he doesn't speak the language, far from his village, his people and the fields of the Punjab.
The British have decided to keep Baba Ram Singh far from anyone who might gather around him.

teach.b: First, the arrest. After Malerkotla, the British took Baba Ram Singh into custody, though Namdhari histories say he hadn't sent the raiders. He wasn't put on trial.
The government used an old regulation that let it hold a person as a state prisoner without charges, and sent him far from the Punjab, across the sea. Second, the place.
Burma was then ruled from British India, and Rangoon was its port city. For a teacher whose whole life was a village, a congregation and the Name recited together, this was very far from home.
He was kept under watch, with few of his own people allowed near. Third, the letters.

Namdharis keep letters said to have been written by Baba Ram Singh in exile and carried back to the Punjab. In them, the community remembers, he encouraged his followers to hold to the Name and to their discipline.
Exile cut the road, but not every thread.

teach.h: WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE END.
teach.b: Fourth, the end, and who says what. British records say he died in Burma. Namdhari tradition holds that he did not die there, and looks for his return.
That belief belongs to the Namdhari community, and this lesson simply reports it.

Punjabi has a word for the one far from home: pardesi, the traveler in a strange land. Some readers of the Guru's hymns hear the soul itself pictured that way, a guest in this world, longing for home.
Baba Ram Singh lived that picture in his body.

how: Namdhari Sikhs remember Baba Ram Singh's exile to Burma, keep letters they hold he wrote from there, and Namdhari tradition looks for his return.

o: a pilgrim on the way to a shrine
a foreigner who rules over others
one far from home, in a strange land

s: Baba Ram Singh was convicted at a trial before his exile
he was held under an old regulation, without trial.
Namdharis keep letters said to be from Baba Ram Singh in exile
the community remembers them urging followers to hold to the Name.
British records and Namdhari belief agree about how his story ended
British records say he died in Burma; Namdhari tradition looks for his return.

games.q: you're Baba Ram Singh, far away in Burma, under watch. your followers are back in the Punjab. what do you do?
o: send letters urging them to hold to the Name.
games.why: Namdharis keep letters said to be his, encouraging them to keep the Name and their discipline.

practice: Bring to mind someone who lives far from home, not by choice: a refugee, a prisoner, someone who can't go back; you don't need their name.
Picture them waking somewhere strange today, and on each breath out, wish them one thing: safety, a letter from home, a familiar voice. If you pray, hold them before Waheguru in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Pardesi, the one far from home, a traveler in a strange land: Baba Ram Singh, held without trial, sent to Rangoon, remembered by his followers through his letters. Today's word.
